pages.text: Trowulan is an old site in East Java. It covers about 100 square kilometres. Experts think this place was once the capital city of the Majapahit Empire. The empire took its name from the city, which was known as Majapahit or Wilwatikta long ago.

Old texts tell us about the capital. A 14th-century poem and a Chinese source describe the royal palace. They talk about thick red brick walls, big gates, and clean buildings. The palace had rooms, courtyards, canals, and spaces for priests and nobles.

Today, many relics are kept in the Trowulan Museum. Visitors can also see old ruins around the village. Some ruins are very damaged, but others have been fixed up. Most of these old buildings are made of red brick.

People have found interesting sites around the area. One of them is Tikus Temple, which is a sunken bathing pool. Another is Wringin Lawang, a large split gate made of red brick. Experts think these structures date back to the Majapahit era.

Archaeologists also found water canals, wells, and housing areas. These finds show that many people lived here long ago. In 2009, the government submitted Trowulan to the UNESCO World Heritage list to help protect the historic site.

B1-B2.headline: Uncovering the Majapahit Capital at Trowulan

pages.text: Trowulan is an archaeological site spanning roughly 100 square kilometres in East Java, Indonesia. Scholars have theorized that this expansive area served as the capital city of the powerful Majapahit Empire. The ancient city was known as Majapahit or Wilwatikta, giving the empire its name.

Historical accounts provide a glimpse into the ancient capital. The 14th-century poem Nagarakretagama and a 15th-century Chinese source describe a walled royal compound featuring large gates, water canals, pavilions, and quarters for priests and nobles. However, because some poetic details are vague, researchers have reached different conclusions when trying to map the capital.

While early research focused mainly on monumental tombs and temples, recent excavations have uncovered industrial areas, commercial zones, water supply systems, and dense habitation sites. Many artifacts from this period are housed in the Trowulan Museum, located near Segaran Pool.

Several notable ruins survive across the landscape. Tikus Temple is a sunken ritual bathing pool featuring terraced structures. Wringin Lawang is a grand red brick split gate from the 14th century, which likely served a ceremonial purpose. Additionally, Brahu Temple stands as the sole surviving structure of a historic building cluster.

Excavations have also revealed brick floors, wells, and drains, indicating an organized urban environment. Economic life was supported by markets using Chinese bronze coins, while clay piggy banks show how people saved money. To protect these historic remnants from damage, Indonesia submitted Trowulan to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2009.

Encompassing approximately 100 square kilometres in the East Java province of Indonesia, Trowulan is an archaeological site widely theorized to be the location of the eponymous capital of the Majapahit Empire. Historically referred to as Majapahit or Wilwatikta, the urban center was ultimately razed during an invasion by Girindrawardhana in 1478, prompting the relocation of the capital to Daha.

Contemporary records, including Mpu Prapanca's 14th-century poem Nagarakretagama and a 15th-century Chinese account, furnish detailed descriptions of the royal compound and urban layout. These texts outline brick fortifications, gates, pavilions, and distinct quarters for nobility and clergy. Because certain poetic descriptions remain ambiguous, scholars compiling capital plans have arrived at divergent interpretations.

Early investigations prioritized monumental religious architecture and tombs, but recent archaeological surveys have identified industrial, commercial, and residential sectors alongside sophisticated water supply networks. These findings collectively indicate a densely populated urban center during the 14th and 15th centuries, with many artifacts subsequently preserved in the Trowulan Museum.

Prominent surviving structures include Tikus Temple, a sunken ritual bathing complex, and Wringin Lawang, a monumental 14th-century split gate constructed from red brick. Furthermore, Brahu Temple is believed to have functioned as a royal mortuary shrine, aligning with local traditions concerning the cremation sites of early Majapahit rulers.

Subsurface excavations have revealed stratified residential remains equipped with wells and drainage systems. Economic activity relied heavily on imported Chinese bronze coins, which replaced previous currencies and facilitated specialized market transactions, as evidenced by the discovery of clay coin containers. In recognition of its immense historical value, Trowulan was submitted to the UNESCO World Heritage list in October 2009.
